sections.takeaway: “Being” can’t be a genus because nothing outside being could divide it into kinds; it is said of things by proportional similarity — each thing’s existence is to its essence as another’s is to its own.
sections.deepDive:
The hardest idea in this section is the argument that **being is not a genus**. It sounds like hair-splitting, but it does real work.

Start with how a genus works. Take “animal.” To mark off a species within it, you add a **specific difference**: “rational” marks off humans; other differences mark off dogs or sharks. Crucially, the difference comes from *outside* the genus. You can understand what “rational” means without already understanding “animal” — there could be rational things that aren’t animals (angels, say). Likewise “having atomic number 79” picks out gold within the genus metal, and you can grasp the atomic number without grasping metalhood.

Now try to treat being as the highest genus, with substance, attribute, and so on as its species. What would the specific difference be? It would have to be something outside being. But whatever is outside being is nothing — and nothing can’t differentiate anything, because it isn’t anything. Put another way: you can’t grasp “substance” or “attribute” without *already* grasping them as ways of being. Their differences are themselves ways of being. So being isn’t divided the way a genus is.

That is why “being” can’t be univocal. A univocal term like “animal” applies in exactly the same way to all its species, with differences added from outside. “Being” applies to everything, and its differences are inside it.

What takes the place of genus and species? **Proportional similarity.** Feser’s example: we “see” a tree and “see” that a theorem is true. The eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem. When we spell out each kind of seeing — light striking the eye versus grasping relations among concepts — they don’t turn out to be two species of one genus. The likeness is in the *relations*.

Applied to being: a man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s existence is to its essence, and as God’s existence is to God’s essence. But the relation differs in each case. In a man and an angel, existence actualizes an essence distinct from it; in God, existence *is* the essence. Feser adds (footnote 14) that being is also said by attribution, with God as the primary analogate.

This section explains why **step 12** must come out as it does, and it lays the groundwork for **step 30**: God isn’t a member of any genus, which is exactly what theistic personalism denies.

The usual confusion: “Being is just the most general category, so everything is a species of it.” The argument shows that picture can’t be right.

checks.q: Why can nothing serve as a specific difference dividing being into species?
options: Because being is too simple to have species
Because the only thing outside being is nonbeing, which cannot differentiate anything
Because only God is a being
Because species exist only in the mind
checks.explanation: A differentia must be extrinsic to its genus, but whatever is extrinsic to being is nothing.

checks.q: What grounds calling both eyesight and intellectual insight “seeing”?
options: They are two species of the genus “seeing”
The eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem — a similarity of relations
Both involve light
The word is used equivocally
checks.explanation: Proportional similarity: the likeness lies in the relations, not in a shared generic nature.

checks.q: In Feser’s proportionality of existence to essence, how does God differ from a man and an angel?
options: God’s existence actualizes a potential essence
God has no essence at all
In God, existence is identical to essence
God’s essence is material
checks.explanation: In creatures existence actualizes a distinct essence; in God they are identical — so the relations differ and predication is analogical.

sections.takeaway: Because potentiality and actuality are both real and really distinct, “real” must apply to them in analogous (neither identical nor unrelated) senses — so being is analogical, on grounds that don’t presuppose God.
sections.deepDive:
The argument has a simple skeleton: it lists the only three options and eliminates two. The hard part is seeing why potentiality is **real but not actual**.

A worked example. Maria is a concert pianist, asleep. Right now she isn’t playing. Is her ability to play something real? Clearly: she differs from someone who has never touched a piano, and that difference is a fact about her now, not just about her past or future. Yet her playing isn’t actual. So her potential is *something* — not nothing — but not the same kind of something as actual playing. That is premise 2 (potency is real) and premise 3 (it is really distinct from act) in one picture.

Now the elimination. If “real” meant exactly the same for Maria’s ability and her actual playing (univocal), there would be no difference between being able to play and playing — potency would just be another actuality (premise 4). If “real” meant something wholly unrelated for her ability (equivocal), then saying her ability is real would be like saying a baseball bat is a “bat” in the zoological sense — i.e., it would really be unreal (premise 5). Since univocal, equivocal, and analogical exhaust literal usage (premise 6), the ability is real in a sense *analogous* to actuality (conclusion 7).

Feser’s defenses matter. Deny premise 2 and you are Parmenides, denying change — incoherent (chapter 1). Deny premise 1 and you are the extreme Heraclitean, for whom only flux exists. But then there is no persisting reasoner to go from premises to conclusion, no stable argument to repeat, no direction to change (a melting ice cube is heading *toward* liquidity and flatness), and no explanation of why things change as they do (ice melts because it is water, not wood or glass). Deny premise 3 by calling the distinction merely verbal, and you collapse into denying premise 1 or 2 — and chapter 4 already gave a real case (essence and existence).

Notice the nuance Feser underlines: the argument needs only act-potency theory, which one could accept *without* accepting any proof of God. That matters dialectically — analogy is not invented to rescue theology.

This section *is* **steps 6–12**. The usual confusion: “potential” means “merely logically possible,” like a unicorn’s being possible. But Aristotelian potency is a real capacity grounded in what something actually is — the ice’s potential to melt, not a mere lack of contradiction.

checks.q: Denying which premise amounts to Parmenides’ denial of change?
options: Actuality is real
Potentiality is real
The three uses exhaust literal usage
If potency were real univocally it wouldn’t be distinct
checks.explanation: Change is the actualization of potential; deny potency and you deny change.

checks.q: Why does Feser hold that if potentiality were real only in an equivocal sense, it wouldn’t be real at all?
options: Because equivocal terms are always false
Because being “real” in a sense wholly unrelated to the ordinary one just means being unreal
Because potentiality is a kind of actuality
Because Heraclitus proved it
checks.explanation: That is premise 5: total unrelatedness of sense leaves nothing of reality.

checks.q: What makes the argument for the analogy of being independent of theism?
options: It relies only on the act/potency distinction, which one can accept without accepting any proof of God
It relies on revelation
It assumes God is the primary analogate
It is a version of the ontological argument
checks.explanation: Feser stresses that the grounds come from act-potency theory alone, so analogy isn’t ad hoc.

sections.takeaway: Univocal God-talk makes God a creature (or leaves only negations), equivocal God-talk leaves words empty — so only analogical predication lets us speak literally and positively about God.
sections.deepDive:
The hardest point here is why **negative theology can’t be the whole story**, even though Feser keeps it as part of the story.

Negative (apophatic) theology describes God by denial: not material, not changing, not in time, not composite. Many attributes in this very chapter are negative in form — immutability (not changing), immateriality (not material), timelessness (not in time). So Feser is not hostile to it. The problem comes if we say *only* negative things. Then we couldn’t say that God exists, or that he causes the world, or that he explains why there is anything at all — every one of those is affirmative. A purely negative theology would undercut the very arguments that led to God.

Why not just speak univocally? Because the proofs lead to something utterly unlike what our words were built for. If “being” *meant* “being a material, changeable thing,” God wouldn’t be a being in that sense. Univocal predication would turn God into one more item of the kind we already know — or, if we refuse that, leave us with only denials.

Why not equivocally? Feser’s fill-in-the-blank test is decisive. Say “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___.” Fill the blank with a univocal term, and the original problem returns. Fill it with an equivocal term, and you have a second word you can’t explain. So equivocation produces not a new meaning but no meaning. The upshot would be agnosticism — or even atheism, if we can’t say what “God exists” means.

A worked comparison: a physicist describing the electron. It isn’t a tiny billiard ball (univocal “particle” misleads), and it isn’t that “particle” means nothing here (equivocal emptiness). Physicists speak of particle-like and wave-like behavior, extending ordinary concepts analogically — just as relativity speaks of curved *space*, though curvature ordinarily belongs to objects in space. Feser draws exactly this parallel: if physics needs analogy, so does talk of the cause of there being a physical world at all.

This section supplies **step 13**, which is used throughout: in answering Plantinga (step 30) and in every positive attribute of Part B.

The usual confusion: “If God-talk is analogical, we don’t really know what we mean.” We know what we affirm (a real perfection of which ours is a limited likeness) and what we deny (the limits and composition it has in us). The concept is indeterminate, not empty.

checks.q: Why can’t negative theology be the whole story, according to Feser?
options: Because negative statements are always false
Because saying that God exists or causes the world is affirmative, so pure negation would undercut the proofs
Because God has no negative attributes
Because negative theology is univocal
checks.explanation: Feser keeps negative theology as part of the truth but notes it can’t express the proofs’ own affirmative conclusions.

checks.q: What is the point of Feser’s “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___” test?
options: To show that God lacks power
To show that any attempt to explain an equivocal term either reintroduces univocity or multiplies unexplained terms
To define power precisely
To show that power is a Cambridge property
checks.explanation: The equivocal option can never be given content, so it leaves God-talk meaningless.

checks.q: Why does Feser mention wave-particle duality and curved space?
options: To show that physics disproves theology
To show that science too extends language analogically beyond ordinary use
To argue that God is a physical field
To prove the universe had a beginning
checks.explanation: If physics needs analogy for strange entities, we should expect it when describing the cause of all physical reality.

sections.bodyAdd: The significance is that “pure actuality” now holds without qualification. Everything that follows — uniqueness, simplicity, immutability, and the rest — depends on there being no potentiality in God *at all*. Had the loophole stayed open, a critic could say that God is unique in his being but changeable, composite, or multiple in his activity. Feser closes it by combining a principle from this chapter (action follows being) with a result from chapter 2 (composites need causes).
sections.takeaway: The First Cause can’t have potentiality even in its activity: acting reflects being, and an actual-plus-potential being would be composite and caused.
sections.deepDive:
The key idea is that **temporal questions and ontological questions come apart**, and the second kind is what matters.

The critic’s proposal: grant that the First Cause’s *existence* needs no actualizing — that’s how it ends the regress — but let its *activity* involve potential. Maybe it has unrealized capacities to do this or that.

Feser’s first reply uses **agere sequitur esse** (step 4). Existence is the most fundamental fact about a thing; everything else about it flows from its being. If a thing’s very being is purely actual, from what in it would merely potential activity arise? Its activities would outrun its nature, which the principle forbids.

His second reply uses chapter 2. A being that is actual in existence but potential in activity has two distinct components: an actual one and a potential one. It is composite. And a composite needs a cause of its composition — something that makes it the case that these parts are united. That cause can’t be one of the parts or the whole itself (that would be self-causation), so it must be external.

Here is where the temporal/ontological distinction enters. A critic may say, “Fine, but suppose the composite always existed — then nothing had to put it together.” Feser replies that the question isn’t *when* the parts were joined but *why they are joined at all*. Course illustration: a lamp has been lit all night. Asking “what’s keeping it lit right now?” is a real question even if it was never switched on (suppose it had always been on); the answer — the current — is **ontologically** prior, not temporally prior. The First Cause, by contrast, has to be what *ends* a hierarchical series of such present dependencies. A first cause that needs a cause isn’t first.

This section is **steps 14–17**. Step 17 — God is purely actual without qualification — is the premise from which unity (step 21), immutability (step 32), immateriality (step 40), and more are derived.

The usual confusion: “If God has no potential, he must be inert or unable to do different things.” Pure actuality means lacking no perfection, not lacking activity; how a purely actual God freely creates is taken up in Part B. Another confusion is to think the argument assumes the universe had a beginning. It doesn’t; it would work in a beginningless world.

checks.q: What is Feser’s first reply to the suggestion that God has potentiality in his activity but not his existence?
options: Activity is unreal
By agere sequitur esse, a purely actual being can’t act in a less than purely actual way
God has no activity
Activity is a Cambridge property
checks.explanation: Action follows being; there’s nothing in a purely actual nature for potential activity to derive from.

checks.q: Why doesn’t it help to suppose the composite First Cause had always existed?
options: Because nothing can always exist
Because the question is why its parts are combined at all, which requires an ontologically (not temporally) prior cause
Because the universe had a beginning
Because eternal things are simple by definition
checks.explanation: Everlastingness removes only a temporally prior cause, not the need for a present uniting cause.

sections.bodyAdd: The conclusion is stronger than it first sounds. Feser isn’t claiming that, as it happens, we only find one God. He is claiming that a second purely actual being is impossible, because nothing could make it a *second* one.
sections.takeaway: There can be many of a kind only where individuals differ by parts, parts entail potency, and so a purely actual being is unique in principle.
sections.deepDive:
The central question is disarmingly simple: **what makes two things two?**

Take two pennies fresh from the mint, identical in design. What makes them two rather than one penny counted twice? Not their nature — both are pennies. Their matter: this lump of copper-coated zinc versus that one. That is how members of a species differ: by the matter in which the shared nature is realized. Now take a penny and a dime. They differ in species (within the genus coin) by some added specific difference — denomination, size, metal. That is how species differ: by a difference added to the genus.

Feser’s claim is that these are the only routes to plurality within a kind, and both require **metaphysical parts**: matter plus form, or genus plus difference. And parts bring **potentiality**. The matter of a penny could have been melted into a wire. The genus coin is, of itself, open to being a penny or a dime; one possibility must be actualized. More generally, parts only potentially make up a whole until something actualizes their union — even if the union never had a first moment.

Feser’s human example makes the same points: animality and rationality are distinct parts of human nature (rationality is one way, not the only way, of being an animal); individual humans differ by matter.

Now apply it. God is purely actual (step 17). So God has no such parts. So there is nothing that could distinguish God from a second God. Footnote 17 closes a loophole: you can’t distinguish two purely actual beings by some *other* kind of part, like substance and accident, because any composition whatsoever entails potency.

This section is **steps 18–21**. Step 21 isn’t just monotheism as a matter of fact — it is monotheism *in principle*. That difference becomes important in the simplicity section, where Feser argues that a God within a genus could be unique only by luck.

The usual confusion: “God is one” is heard as a count — one, like one apple rather than two. But the claim is that God isn’t the kind of thing that could be counted among others at all; he isn’t an instance of a kind. Another confusion is to think two gods could be told apart by location. Location is a feature of material things with parts, which a purely actual being lacks.

checks.q: According to Feser, what distinguishes individual members of a material species, such as two humans?
options: Their specific difference
Their matter
Their essence
Their existence alone
checks.explanation: Members of a species share the nature; matter individuates them.

checks.q: Why does multiplicity within a kind require potentiality?
options: Because it requires parts (matter/form or genus/difference), and parts involve potentiality
Because many things are always in time
Because only material things can be counted
Because PSR forbids plurality
checks.explanation: Matter could be otherwise; a genus is open to several species; parts only potentially compose a whole.

checks.q: Why can’t two purely actual beings be distinguished by one having an accident the other lacks?
options: Because accidents are Cambridge properties
Because any composition, including substance and accident, involves potentiality
Because accidents exist only in material things
Because both would have all accidents
checks.explanation: Footnote 17: parts of any kind entail potency, so neither being would be purely actual.

sections.takeaway: Pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity each entail the others, so the five proofs are five routes to one and the same God.
sections.deepDive:
The hard idea here is **mutual entailment** — and why it settles identity.

In logic, “A if and only if B” means each implies the other: whatever has A has B, and whatever has B has A. Feser establishes a web of such biconditionals:

- purely actual ⇔ absolutely simple;
- purely actual ⇔ subsistent existence itself;
- simple ⇔ subsistent existence itself;
- all three ⇔ absolutely necessary.

Why does this show the proofs reach one being? Because unity (step 21) says there can be only one purely actual being. If everything simple is purely actual, and everything that is subsistent existence is purely actual, and everything necessary is purely actual, then each of these descriptions picks out the one-and-only purely actual being. Five descriptions, one referent.

A course analogy: ancient astronomers named the bright “morning star” and the bright “evening star.” The discovery that both are Venus wasn’t a sixth observation of a new planet; it was the realization that two descriptions pick out one thing. Feser’s convergence works like that, except the identity is shown by reasoning rather than by telescope.

Look at one entailment in detail. Why must something simple be purely actual? It is actual — if it had no actuality it wouldn’t exist. Could it also have some potentiality? Then it would have an actual aspect and a potential aspect, two distinct constituents — and so it wouldn’t be simple. Conversely, why must the purely actual be simple? Because anything with parts has potency: the parts only potentially make up the whole until united.

And necessity: if something were contingent, some potential would need actualizing, or some parts (at least essence and existence) would need combining, for it to exist. Anything with neither exists necessarily. That entailment brings in chapter 5’s necessary being — and chapter 3’s necessarily existing intellect.

This section is **steps 22–26**. Notice that the convergence isn’t a new, sixth argument for God; it’s a consequence of what each proof already concluded plus the analysis of composition and potency.

The usual confusion: “The five proofs are five premises supporting one conclusion, so if one fails the case fails.” In fact each proof is meant to stand alone; convergence shows only that, if more than one succeeds, they reach the same God.

checks.q: Why must something absolutely simple also be purely actual?
options: Because it is material
Because if it had any potentiality it would have an actual part and a potential part, and so not be simple
Because it is in time
Because it is caused
checks.explanation: A simple thing must be actual (or not exist) and can’t mix potency without composition.

checks.q: Which attribute links the Augustinian proof’s divine intellect (ch. 3) to the other proofs’ conclusions?
options: Immateriality
Absolute necessity
Omnipotence
Timelessness
checks.explanation: The necessarily existing intellect of chapter 3 is identified via the entailments between necessity and pure actuality/simplicity/subsistent existence.

checks.q: What is the logical role of the convergence argument?
options: It is a sixth independent proof of God
It shows that the five proofs, if sound, reach one and the same being
It shows that all five proofs depend on each other
It proves that the universe is necessary
checks.explanation: Mutual entailment plus unity shows that the five descriptions pick out one referent.

sections.bodyAdd: Notice the structure of the claim. Feser is not saying simplicity is one more attribute to add to a list. He is saying it is the attribute on which God’s uniqueness and ultimacy depend — so that giving it up doesn’t produce a different conception of God but, strictly, gives up God.
sections.takeaway: Simplicity is inseparable from God’s uniqueness and ultimacy; deny it and God becomes one of a kind and in need of a cause — a superangel, not God.
sections.deepDive:
The hardest point here is Feser’s strong claim that **denying simplicity is implicitly atheism**. That sounds like an insult to theists who reject simplicity; it is actually a precise logical claim.

Recall what “God” means in this book: the ultimate explanation of things, the First Cause that terminates the regress of dependence. Now ask what composition would do. If God had parts of any kind — act and potency, essence and existence, genus and difference, really distinct attributes — then (by chapter 2 and step 16) something would have to account for those parts being united. That something would be more ultimate than God. So the “God” in question would not be the First Cause; the real First Cause would be whatever unites him. Hence: to deny that anything is simple is to deny that anything is ultimate — atheism in Feser’s sense.

Then the uniqueness point. If God fell under a genus, being God would be a kind of thing, and he would be an instance of it. Feser’s Zeus and Odin illustration nails this: even if every other Olympian vanished, Zeus would still be *a* god, the sole survivor of a pantheon. His nature wouldn’t change. So a God within a genus is unique only by luck.

Immateriality doesn’t save the situation. An immaterial being with parts is what Feser calls a **superangel** — powerful, perhaps without body, but still a creature: one of a kind, dependent on a cause. Worshiping it would be idolatry, the honoring of a creature as if it were the Creator.

Feser then notes the breadth of the tradition that held this: Aristotle and Plotinus; Maimonides; Avicenna and Averroes; Athanasius, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas; Lateran IV (1215) and Vatican I (1869–1870); Luther and Calvin. The point isn’t an appeal to authority but a signal that simplicity is the core of classical theism, not a sectarian add-on.

In the formal reasoning, this is **steps 27–28**. Step 27 draws on steps 16 and 18–19; step 28 draws the consequence.

The usual confusion: “simple” heard as “simplistic” or “low in complexity.” Divine simplicity means lack of composition, and it is compatible with — indeed required for — God’s containing all perfections eminently. Another confusion: “Feser says theistic personalists are atheists.” His claim is about the implications of the view, not about anyone’s sincerity.

checks.q: What is the point of the Zeus-alone-on-Olympus illustration?
options: That pagan gods are material
That a god who falls under a kind would be unique only by fact, not in principle
That polytheism is incoherent
That God is immaterial
checks.explanation: Zeus’s nature wouldn’t change if he were the only god left; he’d still be one of a kind.

checks.q: Why does Feser say that denying simplicity implicitly amounts to atheism?
options: Because a composite God would need a cause, so he wouldn’t be the ultimate First Cause
Because theistic personalists deny God exists
Because simplicity is defined by councils
Because composite things can’t be personal
checks.explanation: Composition entails dependence on a uniting cause, which would be more ultimate than the composite ‘God.’

sections.takeaway: Plantinga’s objections come from reading simplicity through univocity, Platonic properties, and a flattened notion of “property”; drop those assumptions and the absurdities vanish, while the real stakes — dependence and uniqueness — remain.
sections.deepDive:
The hardest idea in this section is how God’s power, knowledge, and goodness can be **one reality** without our words becoming synonyms. Plantinga thinks simplicity makes God “one property” and therefore an abstract object. Feser’s reply has several layers; the key is to see how they fit together.

First, **analogy**. In us, power and knowledge really are distinct: you can know how to lift a piano and lack the strength. If “power” and “knowledge” meant exactly the same in God (univocity), their distinctness would carry over. But they are said of God analogically (step 13): God has something that is to his effects as our power is to ours, and something that is to truth as our knowledge is to it. There’s no reason those analogues must be distinct in a being with no parts.

Second, **concepts vs. reality**. Course analogy: “the morning star” and “the evening star” are different concepts, learned through different observations, yet both refer to Venus. Likewise, we form the concept “power” from God’s effects in producing things and “knowledge” from other features of those effects; the concepts differ, but what they apply to in God is one undivided reality.

Third, **constituent ontology**. Plantinga treats properties as abstract Platonic objects that things exemplify. On that view, if God *is* his wisdom, God is an abstract object. But for Aquinas, a thing’s nature and attributes are concrete constituents of it, not items in a third realm. And no classical theist says God is a “property” anyway.

Fourth, **distinguishing kinds of predicates**. Plantinga calls everything a property — being wise, being barefoot, being Plato’s teacher, being Socrates. Aquinas distinguishes essence (rational animality), proper properties (the capacity to be amused), contingent accidents (skin color), and relations (being Plato’s teacher). Lump them together and simplicity seems to make God’s creating humans as essential as his wisdom. Separate them and it doesn’t.

Finally, the **stakes**: a composite God would need a cause and would be unique only contingently — a quasi-divine stand-in, and nothing in the proofs supports such a being. That is why the conclusion of **step 30** holds.

The usual confusion: “simplicity means we can say only one thing about God.” We can say many true things; simplicity concerns what is in God, not how many concepts we use.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of the assumptions Feser says Plantinga reads into the doctrine of simplicity?
options: That properties are Platonic abstract objects
That terms apply to God and creatures univocally
That God has intellect and will
That anything truly predicable of a thing is a property
checks.explanation: Classical theists themselves attribute intellect and will to God; the three problematic assumptions are the other options.

checks.q: What does Wolterstorff’s “constituent ontology” contribute to Feser’s reply?
options: It shows properties are abstract objects
It captures the view that a thing’s nature and attributes are concrete constituents of it, so identifying God with his wisdom doesn’t make him abstract
It proves God is a property
It shows God has many real parts
checks.explanation: Only on a Platonic view would identity with one’s attributes make one an abstract object.

checks.q: How does Feser answer Plantinga’s fallback that it doesn’t matter what we call these features (“characteristics”)?
options: He agrees it is merely verbal
He says Aquinas’ distinctions mark objective metaphysical differences, not preferences about words
He switches to calling them “attributes”
He denies God has any characteristics
checks.explanation: Essence, properties, accidents, and relations really differ; relabeling doesn’t erase that.
